Verification steps

Concrete actions to confirm savings potential.

Apply → Verify
01 — RDS utilization

Gather 30‑ to 90‑day CPU and connection metrics. Flag instances with stable, high utilization as RI candidates and document expected savings for a 1‑year or 3‑year commitment.

screens.title: RDS Reserved Instances
screens.narratorSegment: Reserved Instances for RDS are a commitment-based pricing option where you reserve a specific instance type, database engine, and Region for one or three years. The clear claim is simple: if your relational database runs continuously with predictable capacity, a Reserved Instance reduces hourly costs compared to On‑Demand. A concrete example: a production transactional database serving customer orders 24/7 typically fits an RI because its usage pattern is steady. To decide, analyze at least 30 days of metrics—C P U, memory, storage, and connection counts—and confirm your instance family and Region alignment. A common misconception is that RIs are always better; they are not for test environments, seasonal jobs, or short-lived workloads. Also note that RIs are specific to instance class and Region, so they are less flexible than serverless options. Key trade-offs include the upfront commitment and the need for accurate forecasting, balanced against potentially large percentage savings. Before purchasing, document your expected utilization and a break-even timeline to justify the commitment to finance. Can you identify one RDS instance in your account that meets these criteria? RDS Reserved Instances means reserve for steady, long-running relational databases to reduce hourly cost; not ideal for intermittent or highly variable workloads.. In practical terms, commitment-based savings for predictable relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › RDS Reserved Instances
Definition

What are RDS Reserved Instances?

A purchasing option that locks in a one- or three-year term for a specific RDS instance type, engine, and Region to get discounted hourly pricing versus On‑Demand.

When to use
  • Production databases running 24/7 with stable load.
  • Workloads where instance family and Region are not expected to change.
Common mistake

Buying RIs for short-lived or variable environments; this can increase cost if utilization drops or architecture changes.

Concrete example

A customer has a production RDS MySQL instance used continuously for an e‑commerce site. After analyzing 90 days of metrics and confirming steady utilization, the team purchases a 3‑year RI to reduce hourly cost and reports expected savings to finance.

Key Takeaway

Use RIs only when workload is predictable and long‑running; document utilization and break‑even time before committing.

Check your understanding

If an instance will run 24/7 for a year with steady usage, would an RI likely reduce cost? Why might you still avoid an RI?

screens.title: Amazon Aurora Serverless
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Aurora Serverless is an on-demand configuration for Aurora that automatically starts, scales capacity, and shuts down based on application demand. The essential claim: when database traffic is intermittent, spiky, or infrequent, Serverless can save money because you pay only for the capacity consumed, not for a provisioned instance. A concrete scenario is a development or test database that sits idle most of the day but occasionally runs smoke tests or migrations. In that case, Serverless avoids paying for full-time instances. A common misconception is that Serverless always saves money; it does not for steady, high-throughput workloads where provisioned instances or Reserved Instances will be cheaper. Also consider cold start behavior and connection management when applications expect always-on database connections. The key decision is to match the billing model to workload patterns: use Serverless for variable usage and reserved or provisioned instances for stable production throughput. How might you measure whether Serverless or an RI is cheaper over a quarter? Amazon Aurora Serverless means serverless is cost-efficient for intermittent or spiky relational workloads because capacity scales and you only pay for what you use.. In practical terms, a pay-for-what-you-use option for intermittent relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Amazon Aurora Serverless
Definition

Aurora Serverless

An on‑demand, auto-scaling Aurora configuration that starts and stops and bills by capacity consumed, ideal for applications with variable or infrequent traffic.

When to choose
  • Dev/test databases that are idle most of the time.
  • Event-driven or seasonal workloads with large idle windows.
Concrete example

A reporting service runs nightly jobs and remains idle during the day. Aurora Serverless scales up for the job and scales down afterward, avoiding full‑time instance charges.

Common misconception

Serverless always saves money — not true. For steady, high-traffic databases, provisioned instances with reserved pricing are often cheaper.

Check your understanding

Estimate the billed capacity for a job that runs two hours per day and is idle elsewhere. Would Serverless likely beat a 24/7 provisioned instance?

screens.title: DynamoDB Capacity Modes
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB provides two capacity modes with distinct pricing models and operational trade-offs. On‑Demand charges per read and write request units consumed and automatically scales, making it excellent for new applications or those with unpredictable, spiky traffic. For example, a startup launching a new feature with unknown adoption should start on‑demand to avoid throttling or overprovisioning. Provisioned capacity requires you to set RCUs and WCUs and is suitable when you have predictable, stable traffic; it can be cheaper if you right‑size capacity and use reserved capacity commitments for further discounts. A common error is keeping tables in On‑Demand when traffic steadies: that can be more expensive over time. Conversely, provisioning too aggressively causes waste. The practical approach is to begin On‑Demand, collect a representative period of traffic, then move to Provisioned with Autoscaling or reserved capacity once usage patterns are stable. Always model the expected request volume and compare the estimated monthly costs under both modes before switching. DynamoDB Capacity Modes means start on‑demand for unknown traffic; switch to provisioned with reserved capacity when usage becomes predictable to save cost.. In practical terms, on‑demand vs provisioned — cost model and when to pick each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › DynamoDB Capacity Modes
On‑Demand Capacity

Pay-per-request scalability

Automatically scales to handle any request volume and charges for reads and writes performed. Ideal for unknown or highly variable workloads.

Example

A new API that may see sudden spikes after marketing launches; On‑Demand avoids provisioning mistakes and throttling during spikes.

Provisioned Capacity

Reserved units for predictable traffic

You define RCUs and WCUs; good when traffic is steady. Combine with reserved capacity for discounts over time.

Example

A stable telemetry pipeline that ingests a consistent number of writes per minute, where provisioned capacity reduces per‑unit cost.

Practical decision flow
  1. Start On‑Demand for new or unpredictable tables.
  2. Collect a representative period of traffic metrics.
  3. If traffic stabilizes, calculate needed RCUs/WCUs and compare costs versus On‑Demand.
  4. Consider reserved capacity for long-term predictable usage.
Common mistake

Switching to Provisioned too early or overprovisioning RCUs leads to wasted spend; leaving stable tables on On‑Demand can be more expensive long term.

screens.title: Choosing DynamoDB Mode — Practical steps
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between On‑Demand and Provisioned Capacity is best treated as a short process with measurable steps. First, start new tables in On‑Demand to avoid missed requests and to gather baseline traffic. Second, after a representative period—say 30 to 90 days—analyze peak and average read/write rates to understand variability. Third, model monthly cost estimates for Provisioned with Autoscaling and for On‑Demand using observed averages and peaks. Fourth, if Provisioned shows savings and your traffic patterns are stable enough to justify it, plan a controlled switch and consider reserved capacity to amplify discounts. A concrete example: imagine a table with predictable steady writes of 1000 writes per minute for months—provisioning and reserved capacity will almost always reduce unit costs. A common misconception is that a single high spike invalidates provisioning—don’t forget autoscaling and burst capacity as mitigation. Always include rollback steps and monitor after switching to ensure performance and cost match expectations. Which metric will you check first when evaluating a table? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Choosing DynamoDB Mode
Process

Four-step decision flow

  1. Begin On‑Demand and collect 30–90 days of metrics.
  2. Analyze peak, trough, and steady-state rates.
  3. Model monthly costs for Provisioned vs On‑Demand.
  4. If savings are clear, provision with autoscaling and consider reserved capacity.
Concrete scenario

A logging service receives on average 5,000 reads per minute with small variance. Running cost models shows Provisioned with reserved capacity reduces per-unit cost; the team schedules a weekend change with monitoring and autoscaling enabled to protect against spikes.

Pitfall

Switching without autoscaling or rollback increases risk. Always prepare monitoring and a rollback if throttling appears.

Key Takeaway

Use data, model costs, and automate scaling. Reserve capacity only after traffic stabilizes to maximize savings safely.

screens.title: Data Transfer Costs
screens.narratorSegment: Data transfer costs arise whenever data moves across billing boundaries: out to the internet, between Regions, or sometimes between Availability Zones. The most expensive pattern is data transfer out to the internet, so using a CDN such as CloudFront to cache and serve content from edge locations reduces origin egress. Cross‑Region transfer is often required for multi‑Region replication or global architectures, but it is more costly than keeping compute and storage in a single Region. Inter‑AZ traffic is cheaper but not free and can add up when services chat constantly across AZ boundaries. A useful practice is to group tightly coupled components in the same AZ where latency and cost matter, but maintain multi‑AZ redundancy for critical services. Concrete example: moving large media files from an origin in one Region to users globally will incur high egress; fronting the origin with CloudFront dramatically cuts the origin traffic billed. A common misconception is that internal AWS traffic is always free—confirm whether the flow crosses AZ or Region boundaries. The takeaway is to design with locality and caching to minimize egress charges.

keyIdea.text: Egress to internet, cross‑Region, and inter‑AZ traffic generate costs; use caching and regional design to minimize them.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Data Transfer Costs
Primary cost types
  • Data Transfer Out to Internet: typically the priciest egress.
  • Cross‑Region Transfers: higher than inter‑AZ; used for replication or multi‑Region services.
  • Inter‑AZ Traffic: cheaper but accumulates with chatty services.
Mitigation tactics
  • Use CloudFront to cache content and lower origin egress.
  • Keep data and processing within one Region when possible.
  • Group tightly coupled services by AZ to reduce cross‑AZ chatter.
Concrete example

A media API serving large video files directly from an origin in a single Region experiences heavy internet egress. By placing CloudFront in front of the origin, repeated requests hit edge caches and origin egress is significantly reduced.

Misconception

Assuming internal traffic is always free is risky. Verify whether traffic crosses AZ or Region boundaries, as charges may apply.

Key Takeaway

Design for locality and caching to minimize data transfer charges while preserving availability requirements.

screens.title: NAT Gateway vs VPC Endpoint
screens.narratorSegment: NAT Gateways and VPC Endpoints solve different problems but have distinct cost profiles. A NAT Gateway allows private subnets to reach the internet and is charged hourly plus per‑GB data processing. If your private instances only need to reach AWS services such as S3 or DynamoDB, routing through a NAT Gateway forces traffic through the public path and creates unnecessary data processing costs. VPC Endpoints provide private connectivity to supported AWS services without traversing the public internet. Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free for data transfer and avoid NAT egress charges; Interface Endpoints use PrivateLink and incur endpoint hours and per‑GB charges but still often reduce overall costs and improve security compared to NAT. A practical example is an EC2 instance downloading large files from S3: using a Gateway VPC Endpoint keeps traffic within the AWS network and typically eliminates NAT Gateway data charges. A common trap is leaving a NAT Gateway in place because it was convenient during setup. Always validate whether service traffic can use a VPC Endpoint first. What service calls in your private subnets could be moved to an endpoint?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › NAT Gateway vs VPC Endpoint
NAT Gateway

Provides internet access for private subnets but incurs an hourly charge and per‑GB data processing fees for traffic routed through it.

When NAT makes sense
  • When instances need general internet access for updates or outbound calls to third-party endpoints.
VPC Endpoint

Private connection to supported AWS services. Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB do not have per‑GB transfer charges and avoid NAT egress.

When to use
  • When private instances only need to access AWS services like S3, DynamoDB, or SQS.
Hands-on conceptual activity
Setup with NAT
  1. Create public and private subnets.
  2. Deploy NAT Gateway in public subnet with an Elastic IP.

  2. Create Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 and attach to the route table.

screens.title: Audit Unused Network Resources
screens.narratorSegment: Unused or underutilized network resources are a frequent source of recurring costs. Elastic IPs, for example, are free only while associated with a running EC2 instance; if left unattached you incur a small hourly charge. Idle load balancers still incur hourly and data processing fees. VPN connections and Direct Connect circuits carry recurring charges even when they are idle. VPC Flow Logs create storage costs in S3 or CloudWatch Logs if retention or lifecycle policies are not configured. A practical audit process starts by listing all network resources and filtering by last-used date or association status: unattached EIPs, load balancers with no active targets, VPNs with no recent traffic, and Flow Logs with never‑expiring retention. For each flagged item, either document why it must remain or schedule deletion and implement a lifecycle plan for logs. A common mistaken belief is that resources created by earlier teams are harmless; in reality they generate continuous charges. Your audit checklist should include the expected owner and a deletion timeline to ensure savings are realized. Which idle resource would you remove first and why?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Audit Unused Network Resources

Audit checklist for network cleanup

A repeatable process to find and remove resources that cause recurring costs.

Elastic IPs (EIPs)

Identify EIPs that are not associated with running instances and release them. Unattached EIPs incur hourly charges.

Load balancers

Find ALBs/NLBs with no healthy targets or no recent traffic. Terminate unused load balancers to stop hourly and data processing costs.

VPN & Direct Connect

List connections with little or no traffic and confirm whether they are needed. Decommission if no longer required.

VPC Flow Logs

Check retention for Flow Logs stored in S3 or CloudWatch. Implement lifecycle rules to archive or delete old logs and reduce storage costs.

Action plan
  1. Tag each flagged resource with owner and cost impact.
  2. Document justification or schedule deletion within a timeline.
  3. Implement alerts and lifecycle rules to prevent reoccurrence.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two cost-heavy areas of cloud bills: managed databases and network traffic. You will learn practical rules of thumb for when to commit to a reserved database instance, when to use an on-demand serverless database, and how DynamoDB capacity modes change your cost model. We also explore networking traps: the real cost of NAT Gateways, the savings from VPC Endpoints, and how data moving between Availability Zones, Regions, or out to the internet drives charges. Each concept includes an example you can reason about in your architectural reviews. For example, we’ll contrast reserving an RDS instance for a steady production workload versus using Aurora Serverless for an intermittent pipeline. You’ll also get a hands-on conceptual activity comparing NAT Gateway costs with a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3. By the end, you’ll be able to identify the largest database and network savings opportunities and justify small upfront commitments when they lead to large long-term savings. What is one network charge you can check in your next cost report?

These objectives guide what you will be able to do after completing the chapter. First, you will learn how to select cost‑saving options for relational databases, including when a Reserved Instance is appropriate and when Aurora Serverless is a better fit. Second, you will understand DynamoDB pricing so you can choose between on‑demand and provisioned capacity based on read/write patterns. Third, you will identify the main sources of data transfer costs and concrete techniques to reduce them, like using CloudFront or keeping traffic within a Region. Fourth, you will implement cost‑effective networking by choosing VPC Endpoints over NAT Gateways when private access to AWS services suffices, and by auditing unused networking resources. Each objective includes a concrete milestone so you can verify competency by running account checks and cost reports. Treat these objectives as actionable checks you can perform in a review or communications with your finance team.

These hands‑on objectives translate the chapter into account checks you can run. You will be able to identify steady RDS instances that are good RI candidates by checking utilization and uptime. You will know how to evaluate a DynamoDB table’s traffic—when it’s still experimental, start on‑demand; when traffic stabilizes, consider provisioned capacity with reserved units. You’ll learn how to inspect data egress and inter‑Region transfer in billing reports, and to use a caching layer like CloudFront to reduce repeated origin transfers. Finally, you’ll be able to scan for idle network resources such as unattached Elastic IPs, unused load balancers, stale VPNs, and excessive Flow Log storage, then take corrective action. Each objective includes a verification step you can document and present to a finance stakeholder. Practice these checks to build a repeatable cost optimization review process.

Reserved Instances for RDS are a commitment-based pricing option where you reserve a specific instance type, database engine, and Region for one or three years. The clear claim is simple: if your relational database runs continuously with predictable capacity, a Reserved Instance reduces hourly costs compared to On‑Demand. A concrete example: a production transactional database serving customer orders 24/7 typically fits an RI because its usage pattern is steady. To decide, analyze at least 30 days of metrics—C P U, memory, storage, and connection counts—and confirm your instance family and Region alignment. A common misconception is that RIs are always better; they are not for test environments, seasonal jobs, or short-lived workloads. Also note that RIs are specific to instance class and Region, so they are less flexible than serverless options. Key trade-offs include the upfront commitment and the need for accurate forecasting, balanced against potentially large percentage savings. Before purchasing, document your expected utilization and a break-even timeline to justify the commitment to finance. Can you identify one RDS instance in your account that meets these criteria? RDS Reserved Instances means reserve for steady, long-running relational databases to reduce hourly cost; not ideal for intermittent or highly variable workloads.. In practical terms, commitment-based savings for predictable relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Amazon Aurora Serverless is an on-demand configuration for Aurora that automatically starts, scales capacity, and shuts down based on application demand. The essential claim: when database traffic is intermittent, spiky, or infrequent, Serverless can save money because you pay only for the capacity consumed, not for a provisioned instance. A concrete scenario is a development or test database that sits idle most of the day but occasionally runs smoke tests or migrations. In that case, Serverless avoids paying for full-time instances. A common misconception is that Serverless always saves money; it does not for steady, high-throughput workloads where provisioned instances or Reserved Instances will be cheaper. Also consider cold start behavior and connection management when applications expect always-on database connections. The key decision is to match the billing model to workload patterns: use Serverless for variable usage and reserved or provisioned instances for stable production throughput. How might you measure whether Serverless or an RI is cheaper over a quarter? Amazon Aurora Serverless means serverless is cost-efficient for intermittent or spiky relational workloads because capacity scales and you only pay for what you use.. In practical terms, a pay-for-what-you-use option for intermittent relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DynamoDB provides two capacity modes with distinct pricing models and operational trade-offs. On‑Demand charges per read and write request units consumed and automatically scales, making it excellent for new applications or those with unpredictable, spiky traffic. For example, a startup launching a new feature with unknown adoption should start on‑demand to avoid throttling or overprovisioning. Provisioned capacity requires you to set RCUs and WCUs and is suitable when you have predictable, stable traffic; it can be cheaper if you right‑size capacity and use reserved capacity commitments for further discounts. A common error is keeping tables in On‑Demand when traffic steadies: that can be more expensive over time. Conversely, provisioning too aggressively causes waste. The practical approach is to begin On‑Demand, collect a representative period of traffic, then move to Provisioned with Autoscaling or reserved capacity once usage patterns are stable. Always model the expected request volume and compare the estimated monthly costs under both modes before switching. DynamoDB Capacity Modes means start on‑demand for unknown traffic; switch to provisioned with reserved capacity when usage becomes predictable to save cost.. In practical terms, on‑demand vs provisioned — cost model and when to pick each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deciding between On‑Demand and Provisioned Capacity is best treated as a short process with measurable steps. First, start new tables in On‑Demand to avoid missed requests and to gather baseline traffic. Second, after a representative period—say 30 to 90 days—analyze peak and average read/write rates to understand variability. Third, model monthly cost estimates for Provisioned with Autoscaling and for On‑Demand using observed averages and peaks. Fourth, if Provisioned shows savings and your traffic patterns are stable enough to justify it, plan a controlled switch and consider reserved capacity to amplify discounts. A concrete example: imagine a table with predictable steady writes of 1000 writes per minute for months—provisioning and reserved capacity will almost always reduce unit costs. A common misconception is that a single high spike invalidates provisioning—don’t forget autoscaling and burst capacity as mitigation. Always include rollback steps and monitor after switching to ensure performance and cost match expectations. Which metric will you check first when evaluating a table? Choosing DynamoDB Mode — Practical steps means follow a measured analysis: start on‑demand, gather data, model costs, then switch to provisioned with reserved capacity if savings are clear.. In practical terms, a short process to decide and transition safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Data transfer costs arise whenever data moves across billing boundaries: out to the internet, between Regions, or sometimes between Availability Zones. The most expensive pattern is data transfer out to the internet, so using a CDN such as CloudFront to cache and serve content from edge locations reduces origin egress. Cross‑Region transfer is often required for multi‑Region replication or global architectures, but it is more costly than keeping compute and storage in a single Region. Inter‑AZ traffic is cheaper but not free and can add up when services chat constantly across AZ boundaries. A useful practice is to group tightly coupled components in the same AZ where latency and cost matter, but maintain multi‑AZ redundancy for critical services. Concrete example: moving large media files from an origin in one Region to users globally will incur high egress; fronting the origin with CloudFront dramatically cuts the origin traffic billed. A common misconception is that internal AWS traffic is always free—confirm whether the flow crosses AZ or Region boundaries. The takeaway is to design with locality and caching to minimize egress charges.

NAT Gateways and VPC Endpoints solve different problems but have distinct cost profiles. A NAT Gateway allows private subnets to reach the internet and is charged hourly plus per‑GB data processing. If your private instances only need to reach AWS services such as S3 or DynamoDB, routing through a NAT Gateway forces traffic through the public path and creates unnecessary data processing costs. VPC Endpoints provide private connectivity to supported AWS services without traversing the public internet. Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free for data transfer and avoid NAT egress charges; Interface Endpoints use PrivateLink and incur endpoint hours and per‑GB charges but still often reduce overall costs and improve security compared to NAT. A practical example is an EC2 instance downloading large files from S3: using a Gateway VPC Endpoint keeps traffic within the AWS network and typically eliminates NAT Gateway data charges. A common trap is leaving a NAT Gateway in place because it was convenient during setup. Always validate whether service traffic can use a VPC Endpoint first.
